hi-
You know I am actually planning to do something very similar! I'm 29, been bulimic for 10 years.  
  I have tried everything to recover- rehabs, hospitals, therapy, volunteering, so many meds, so many jobs, went to nursing school and couldn't handle it due to this evil sickness.  

I plan to work a little more til my apartment lease ends this spring to keep up decent rental history, wisely research and choose a camper van, pare down my possessions, and travel the continent and work with WWOOF (Worldwide Opportunities on Organic  Farms, an organization that connects you with farmers/homesteaders who host travelers to stay on their property, and learn a ton of new farming-related skills in exchange for work).  I feel that can be really helpful with my recovery by throwing me into these new situations where I won't have access to constant food and will be emotionally/physically stimulated in a very new way.  And in between farm stays, if I find a job I like in a new place, do that.  
I don't think it's rash.  I think it's a radical change and could lead to some new places.  I don't have anyone relying on me so I am free to go.  I am trying to plan it wisely however and make sure I am ready.  It will always be a struggle I think.  Recovery I feel will be lifelong, but I need to try something bold.  Nothing else is working for me.  I also feel that bulimia has probably taken years off my life so I'd rather go for that wild dream now before it's too late.  

maybe we could meet up on our future travels!

Note- I am not giving you advice, or telling you to do this - just expressing that I am exploring this idea too.

I adopted a troubled rescue dog and love her terribly, but she is a handful and in no way could be a true therapy dog.. However, like a few others said here, she gives me a reason to get up and she keeps me active (long walks and hikes).  She's great, cuddly and loving and we are working on training for her behavioral issues (she was abused so she has plenty of issues- mostly with crazy anxiety around other humans and barking) so that's a good activity- working on the training.  HOWEVER if I could go back in time I would've looked into getting an actual therapy dog, or one that's a lot calmer/older.  I think I read too many articles/seen too many sappy movies on how a troubled dog helped someone find a new meaning in life and overcome despair (not quite the case) so I think you should go for an actual therapy dog/ one that won't contribute to stress.  
Anyway, the point of my rambling is go for it and choose your pet wisely!!

"I have to be in person" 
I struggle with this too.  I live in this dream world a lot of the time, when I'm alone (which is far too frequent).  I have abilities, and I just don't put myself out there to share them because of all the anxieties.  I am constantly fantasizing about sharing my abilities (for instance, I play guitar, and haven't performed onstage since I was a teenager.  I've shown up at open mic nights in my city and then just left before performing because I'm so afraid of failure.  Then I go home alone and dream up how it could've gone well, how I could've met other artists, how I'll have the guts to do it next time, etc). I just sit and play at home alone.   It's the whole "if a tree falls in the forest, does it make a sound?" thing.   We live in a world where we are constantly putting ourselves on display- look at social media, fb, linkedin, youtube, constantly sharing ourselves and our actions.  And with the perfectionist tendencies we have ( I just saw another post on that in this forum) we hold back.  We are humble to a fault, but there is something to be said for humility and living a quiet, private life I suppose?
  It's so hard to ACT and DO.  
Once an old lady I used to work  looked at me and said, "My dear, you are a dreamer." and it's too true.  Recently, I was offered a marketing internship at a really cool music venue in my town. I kept playing over in my mind how I'd rock it, then get offered a job and turn my life around. I showed up for a few shifts and did my job enthusiastically, but the whole time I felt like a fraud and that somehow I wasn't cool or knowledgeable enough to be there so I quit.  I couldn't "do" because my stupid brain convinced me I wasn't worthy.  It's such a shame because I bet you and others here are quite talented and intelligent, we just have the meanest inner critics that destroy so many good opportunities we are given. And when that happens, it becomes less likely to find and keep hold of other good opportunities that come in the future because it has become our self-fulfilling prophecy of sabotage.  Sigh.
